content: There are no additional monitoring and evaluation considerations beyond those outlined in the following WHO guidelines: the WHO treatment guidelines for drug-resistant tuberculosis; 2016 update, the Use of bedaquiline in the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis: interim policy guidance, and the Use of delamanid in the treatment of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis: interim policy guidance. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) identified several research priorities: 1. Further research is needed to evaluate whether a 4-month fluoroquinolone-containing regimen could be non-inferior to the standard regimen in specific populations, such as individuals with a body mass index (BMI) greater than 18 or those with non-severe, non-cavitary tuberculosis disease. The optimal dosing of fluoroquinolones must be determined, as higher doses may influence treatment outcomes. Investigations should focus on why certain groups experience worse outcomes with a 4-month fluoroquinolone-containing regimen. Biological mechanisms underlying Mycobacterium tuberculosis persistence and disease recurrence, despite faster culture conversion with certain regimens, should be explored. More qualitative research and systematic reviews are required to understand patient values and preferences regarding tuberculosis treatment regimens. 2. The effectiveness of fixed-dose combination (FDC) tuberculosis treatments compared to separate drug formulations in patients with drug-susceptible tuberculosis should be further studied. Additional research is needed to understand why FDC formulations have not demonstrated clear benefits over separate drug formulations. Pharmacokinetic studies should assess the bioavailability of FDCs versus separate drug formulations, and weight-banding categories for drug dosing should be improved. The optimal dose of rifampicin, including its use in different drug formulations, should be determined. Further qualitative studies are needed to examine medication adherence. Efforts should focus on improving FDC formulations to reduce pill burden, particularly for patients with co-morbidities. 3. Research should address the optimal duration of the intensive phase of therapy. Additional studies are needed to evaluate the benefits of thrice-weekly dosing during the continuation phase, as differences in outcomes between thrice-weekly and daily dosing during this phase are minimal. 4. Studies should explore etiological factors contributing to higher mortality and adverse event rates in HIV-positive tuberculosis patients, including factors such as late initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), low CD4 cell counts, tuberculosis drug resistance, cumulative drug toxicity, and drug-drug interactions with newer antiretroviral drugs. 5. The use of steroids in the treatment of extrapulmonary tuberculosis requires further investigation. The optimal steroid dose for tuberculosis meningitis, including different drug formulations, should be determined. The optimal duration of steroid therapy for tuberculosis meningitis should be established, considering whether this duration varies by the severity of meningitis. The differential effects of steroids on HIV-positive versus HIV-negative individuals, as well as those receiving ART, should be studied. The relationship between steroid treatment and cancer risk, as highlighted in studies such as Mayosi et al. on pericarditis, should be examined. 6. The effectiveness of various interventions to improve treatment adherence should be evaluated. Research should identify patient support and treatment supervision interventions best suited to specific populations. Studies should determine which patient support interventions are most effective in lowand middle-income countries. Cost-effectiveness analyses of different types of incentives should be conducted. The effectiveness of video-observed therapy (VOT) in lowand middle-income countries should be studied, as current data primarily come from high-income countries. Research should identify the most appropriate types of psychological support for patients. 7. The risk of tuberculosis transmission associated with hospital-centered care versus outpatient clinics should be assessed. Additional cost-effectiveness studies comparing decentralized and centralized care models are needed. Programs providing decentralized care should be encouraged to publish or systematically collect their data to inform future research and policy development.
